thread.title: PBP: Why This Buy-Write ETF Has Been Uninspiring - Invesco S&P 500 BuyWrite Portfolio ETF (NYSEARCA:PBP)

author: D.M. Martins Research
title: PBP: Why This Buy-Write ETF Has Been Uninspiring - Invesco S&P 500 BuyWrite Portfolio ETF (NYSEARCA:PBP)
text:
Just recently, I wrote my first article on buy-write ETFs - also referred to as covered call funds. The security that I analyzed in a bit more detail was the Horizons NASDAQ 100 Covered Call ETF ( QYLD ). I was intrigued by some of my findings, and decided to look for the "best in class" fund within this investment category.
I turned to the U.S. News and World Report's ranking of best options-based funds for inspiration. At the top of the list was the Invesco S&P 500 BuyWrite ETF ( PBP ). The fund is said to "invest at least 90% of its total assets in securities that comprise the underlying index (a hypothetical 'buy-write' strategy on the S&P 500 index) and will write/sell call options thereon."
Credit: Argaam
Not as good as it seemed at first But the yellow flags started to come up before I even left the Seeking Alpha site. Other authors have covered this ETF in the past, and the consensus so far has been to avoid this particular fund. Something didn't add up in my mind, as U.S. News ranked PBP at the top of its category and Morningstar has it listed as a five-star fund.
A quick peek at Invesco's page revealed that the ETF's past performance has in fact been pretty lackluster. See graph below, and notice that:
PBP has lagged the S&P 500 ( SPY ) by quite a bit. Over the past 10 years, $10,000 invested in a plain basket of stocks in late 2008 would have been worth today nearly twice as much as the same hypothetical amount invested in PBP. Not so evident in the graph below, the buy-write index that PBP tracks has produced inferior risk-adjusted performance as well: Sharpe ratio of 0.59 vs. the S&P 500's 0.81, as of Sept. 30, 2018, (the gap has probably narrowed, following the fourth quarter broad market correction). PBP has trailed the performance of the buy-write index (pink vs. purple lines below). However, the difference appears to be minimal and likely explained by the compounding of the ETF's 0.49% annual management fee. Source: Invesco's fund performance page
The facts and figures above tell a very different story from what I observed when I analyzed QYLD a few days ago. I dug deeper into PBP's prospectus to try and find out why it has done so much more poorly than its close cousin. But not much seems to differ between the two funds with regard to their strategy or methodology.
What may explain the lackluster results However, I do have a hypothesis that might explain PBP's historical under performance.
I had previously estimated that, in a covered call strategy, most of the investment gains come in the form of call option premium collected. In the Apple ( AAPL ) example that I presented last time , assuming the stock climbs 20% in market value through January 2020, I calculate that nearly two thirds of the buy-write play's returns of 12% would come in the form of net option premium earned. In other words, selling pricey calls is perhaps the most important piece of the whole strategy, at least in what pertains to expected returns.
The bad news for PBP is that the S&P 500, better diversified and less concentrated in more aggressive sectors like technology, is generally perceived to be less risky than the Nasdaq 100. With lower volatility expectations comes lower option prices, therefore lower premium generated by the buy-write investor. For example, buying the Nasdaq index ( QQQ ) at-the-money options that expire in January 2020 costs today about 14% of the underlying security's notional value. By comparison, it costs only 9% to do the same in the case of the S&P 500 index. The five percentage point difference in annual return between the two can certainly make a difference in the success of the investment strategies.
A few takeaways Once again, these are my first few steps as I venture into the world of buy-write (or covered call) ETFs. But I already have a few preliminary conclusions drawn from my initial observations:
The investment strategy may be able to beat the broad market on a risk-adjusted basis over the long run, although guarantees can not be offered. Using lower volatility indices like the S&P 500 may produce inferior results vs. doing the same with higher volatility indices like the Nasdaq 100. Blindingly trusting well-regarded publications like U.S. News and Morningstar and their ratings on ETFs can lead the less diligent investor to make costly mistakes - caution is highly advised.
